top.line: Two AI sessions that share nothing passed keys, a certificate, images and an encrypted message through QR codes I screenshotted.
top.para: In three hours: text, signed JSON, keys, an X.509 certificate, images, then a key exchange. The 2,953-byte maximum decoded from a screenshot at 1.3 pixels a square, byte-identical to the original. The failures matter too: no reading by eye, the decoder mattered, a key was lost. QR codes beat blobs of text for moving keys.

in-short.line: Seven lines: no shared anything, the limit, nothing lost, keys and images, encryption, failures, friendlier.
in-short.para: The only link was me. One code holds 2,953 bytes and it decoded from a screenshot. Every payload matched byte for byte. Keys, a certificate and a 539-byte infographic fitted. A public key went out and an encrypted message came back. The failures taught the most. QR codes are friendlier than blobs of text.

question.line: A serendipitous question: could two sessions with nothing shared talk through QR codes and a person?
question.para: Session A generated codes and Session B decoded and verified them, in two browser tabs with no shared memory, network link or files. The connection was me: a screenshot, a paste, and later a ZIP. Both sessions wrote debriefs, and this article is built from them and their data.

layers.line: Up a layer each time: text, signed JSON, keys and a certificate, binary and images, then encryption.
layers.para: An Ed25519 signature still verified after the trip; Ed25519, P-256 and RSA keys and an X.509 certificate parsed and checked; images rebuilt from their bytes. A graded test set of eleven codes, from 53 bytes to the maximum, each with its own hash, all decoded and matched a separate manifest.

screenshot.line: One screenshot of four codes, pasted into the other tab: all four decoded, byte for byte.
screenshot.para: Through a browser's scaling, a Retina screenshot and a clipboard. The version 40 code, 177 by 177 squares in about 230 pixels, about 1.3 pixels a square, decoded first time. Compared with the originals later, every payload was identical: QR error correction absorbed what the screenshot did.

capacity.line: 2,953 bytes is the ceiling; elliptic-curve keys are tiny; compression did not help; encoding matters.
capacity.para: An Ed25519 key is 43 characters and RSA-4096 still fits at 800. A zlib-compressed certificate came out larger than an RSA-4096 key, since signed data is near random. Raw bytes hold most but many decoders corrupt them; base45 costs about 3% and survives everywhere.

images.line: A whole infographic in 539 bytes as compressed SVG; a photo-like image in 2,083 as AVIF.
images.para: The SVG came back exact and sharp at any size, about a fifth of one code. The 480 by 320 image was generated for the test. As raster the infographic needed 1,881 to 2,810 bytes and lost detail: for anything drawn, vector wins by far.

exchange.line: Session B published an X25519 key as a QR code; Session A encrypted and signed a message to it; B decrypted it.
exchange.para: QRE1 frames: a fresh ephemeral key per message, ChaCha20-Poly1305, an Ed25519 signature, 1,329 bytes in one code, fingerprint aab8 bef5 confirmed first. I carried a public key one way and ciphertext the other, so email or chat would have done as well.

failures.line: The failures: no reading by eye, the decoder over resolution, a lost key, integrity not authenticity.
failures.para: Session A said plainly it could not decode by looking. OpenCV failed on dense codes; ZXing read them all, and Session B corrected its own explanation. A private key kept only in memory was lost, and Session A signed with a new key and said so. A signature proves bytes, not senders.

why.line: QR codes are friendlier than blobs of text, and point to a client-side channel on public keys.
why.para: In the memo: way more user friendly than what we used to share vault keys and encrypted messages. It extends send to my vault, the ways a secret moves on public keys, and the directory of keys. Today measured the channel; the workflow and who else does this come next.

limits.line: No reading by vision, no proof of sender, a new key not yet accepted, not forward-secret, an experiment.
limits.para: A library decodes. Authenticity needs a fingerprint check or pinning on first use. The new signing key waited on my check. Session B's key is long-lived, so not forward-secret. Keys lived in cloud sessions. About 2.9 KB a code; more needs several codes.

sources.line: The two sessions' debriefs, their data, scripts and images, and my voice memo of the same afternoon.
sources.para: Session A's debrief pack with results, manifest, scripts and images; Session B's briefing and its QRE1 format; my voice memo of 21 October 2026. All images were made in the experiment.
